summary: Defines a URN namespace for 3GPP2 and a namespace-specific string for the Mobile Equipment Identity (MEID), a 15-hexadecimal-digit identifier that uniquely identifies a mobile device.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8464 gives a standard web-style name to the identity number that a 3GPP2 mobile handset carries. The name has the form urn:3gpp2:meid: followed by the maker's code and the device's serial number. The RFC also states that the number must not be treated as a secret, because anyone holding the handset can read it.

subtitle: A standard URN name for the identity number that 3GPP2 mobile equipment carries.

tldr.problem: Mobile equipment in 3GPP2 networks carries a Mobile Equipment Identity (MEID) whose encoding and format differ from the 3GPP IMEI, so the URN namespace defined for the IMEI cannot represent it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the '3gpp2' URN namespace with IANA and defines a namespace-specific string that writes an MEID as urn:3gpp2:meid: followed by the 8-digit manufacturer code, a hyphen and the 6-digit serial number, leaving out the check digit.
tldr.outcome: Internet protocols can now name a 3GPP2 handset in a standard way, and the RFC sets firm limits on how that identifier may be used, since anyone with the handset can read it.

facts.label: Check digit
facts.value: 1 hexadecimal digit, not transmitted and not in the URN

today: RFC 8464 is an Informational document from September 2018. IANA has registered the 3gpp2 URN namespace using the template it contains, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it, so the namespace and the meid namespace-specific string it defines remain the standard way to name a 3GPP2 MEID as a URN.

sections.title: Why 3GPP2 Needs Its Own Namespace
sections.content:
Mobile equipment that is single-mode 3GPP, using only 3GPP technology to transmit and receive voice or data, or dual-mode 3GPP/3GPP2, has an International Mobile station Equipment Identity (IMEI). A URN namespace and a namespace-specific string for the IMEI are defined in RFC 7254, and for dual-mode 3GPP2 access that IMEI URN can identify the equipment.

Single-mode 3GPP2 mobile equipment that supports only 3GPP2 access technology instead has a hexadecimal MEID. Because there are fundamental differences between the MEID and the IMEI, in encoding, format and ownership, the URN defined in RFC 7254 cannot be used to represent a hexadecimal MEID.

This document specifies a URN namespace for 3GPP2 and a namespace-specific string for the MEID, fulfilling the 3GPP2 requirement to be able to use an MEID as a URN. The Namespace Identifier is 3gpp2, for identities used in 3GPP2 networks, and it is managed by 3GPP2. The specification defines only namespace-specific strings constructed from MEIDs under this identifier; these start with meid: so that they can be recognized as such. The 3GPP2 may specify other kinds of namespace-specific string under the same identifier in the future.

The RFC also warns that the MEID and the IMEI are separate identifiers and are not to be confused, and that Internet implementations will not generally possess MEID identifiers. Identifiers generated by such implementations will typically be URNs in namespaces other than 3gpp2, and may in some contexts be non-URN URIs, so implementations are advised to be ready to process URIs outside this namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mobile network standards identify handsets differently. The 3GPP number already has a standard name, but the 3GPP2 number is formatted differently, so it needed a namespace of its own before Internet protocols could pass it around.

sections.title: The Registered Namespace and Its Syntax
sections.content:
The namespace identifier is 3gpp2, at version 1, registered on 2018-06-10 by the Third Generation Partnership Project 2, with the contact given as the MEID Global Hexadecimal Administrator and the TIA TR-45 EUMAG Chair. The purpose recorded in the registration is to identify mobile equipment using technologies defined by 3GPP2, initially by a URN that embeds a 15-digit MEID unique to each individual piece of equipment.

The identifier is expressed in ASCII characters and has a hierarchical expression using Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF), as defined in RFC 5234. The ABNF is reproduced below.

The namespace-specific string for an MEID contains one meidval, which is the manufacturer code, a hyphen, and the serial number. The manufacturer code is 8HEX and the serial number is 6HEX, where HEX is a digit or an upper-case letter from A to F. The future-pp2-specifier production reserves room for other namespace-specific strings that 3GPP2 may define later under the same identifier.

Identifiers in the 3gpp2 namespace are defined and assigned by 3GPP2 or an agency appointed by it, after ensuring that the URNs to be assigned are unique. Procedures are in place to ensure that each MEID is uniquely assigned by the manufacturer. The manufacturer code and serial number are permanently stored in the mobile equipment, so they persist for as long as the equipment exists, and the values once assigned are never reassigned to other pieces of equipment. No resolution is envisioned for these URNs.

RFC 8465, published at the same time, specifies how the MEID URN can be used as an Instance ID. The RFC gives an example of a 3GPP2 MEID URN: urn:3gpp2:meid:A04B0D56-02A7E3.
sections.plainLanguage: The name follows a fixed grammar. It starts with urn, then the namespace 3gpp2, then meid, then the maker's 8-digit code, a hyphen and the 6-digit serial number. The two parts are written in upper-case hexadecimal, so they use the letters A to F as digits as well as 0 to 9.

sections.title: The Parts of an MEID
sections.content:
The MEID is 15 hexadecimal digits long and is defined by 3GPP2 to uniquely identify each individual piece of mobile equipment, such as a handset or mobile phone. It has three parts.

The manufacturer code is 8 hexadecimal digits and identifies the mobile equipment manufacturer. It is chosen from a range of values allocated to the manufacturer, so that the manufacturer is uniquely identified. A manufacturer can be assigned more than one manufacturer code.

The serial number is 6 hexadecimal digits and identifies equipment within the manufacturer code, so the pair of manufacturer code and serial number identifies one handset.

The check digit is a single hexadecimal digit, the first 4 bits of octet 8. It is used as assurance of integrity in error-prone operations, for example when the MEID is used with certain types of readers during inventory-management operations. The check digit is not transmitted by the mobile equipment, so the first 14 of the 15 hexadecimal digits are used when the MEID is written as a URN.

Any future change to the format of the meid namespace-specific string would require the URN NSS change procedure, currently the publication of a future Informational RFC approved by IETF consensus. A change to the Instance ID described in RFC 8465 would require an update to that RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The identity number has three parts: 8 digits for the maker, 6 digits for the device within that maker, and one check digit. The check digit catches errors when the number is read by a scanner during inventory work, and it is not sent over the air, so it is left out of the URN.

sections.title: Hexadecimal Encoding in Eight Octets
sections.content:
The MEID format is 15 hexadecimal digits encoded in 8 octets. The most significant digit of the manufacturer code is encoded in the first 4 bits of octet 1, and the most significant digit of the serial number is encoded in the first 4 bits of octet 5. The check digit occupies the first 4 bits of octet 8, and the remaining 4 bits of octet 8 are zero-padded, because only 4 bits are needed to encode the check digit.

When the MEID is included in a cellular signaling message, the check digit is omitted and only the first 7 octets are transmitted.

The RFC presents a figure as an abstract representation of a hexadecimal-encoded MEID stored in memory, and notes that the actual storage format in memory is implementation specific. The information in the RFC is meant to be a concise guide for those wishing to use the hexadecimal MEID as a URN, and nothing in it overrides the 3GPP2 specification that defines the MEID itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the handset the 15-digit number is held in 8 bytes. Each hexadecimal digit takes 4 bits, so the check digit needs only half of the last byte, and the other half is left as zero. On the network the check digit is dropped, so 7 bytes go out.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Rules
sections.content:
An MEID is usually printed outside of the box in which the mobile device ships, and may also be printed under the battery, although very few devices have removable batteries today. It can be retrieved through the device settings or by dialing *#06#. Anyone with brief physical access to the device or its box can easily obtain the MEID. MEIDs MUST NOT therefore be used as security capabilities, meaning identifiers whose mere possession grants access. The RFC notes that there are currently examples of some applications using the MEID for authorization, and that some service providers' customer service departments have been known to use knowledge of the MEID as proof that the caller is the legitimate owner of the device. Both are described as inappropriate uses of the MEID.

Since the MEID is permanently assigned to the mobile equipment and is not modified when the ownership of the equipment changes, even on a complete software reload, the MEID URN MUST NOT be used as a user identifier or user address by an application. Using it that way could result in communications destined for a previous owner being received by the new owner, or could let the new owner reach information or services owned by the previous owner.

Because the MEID identifies the mobile equipment, it could also be used to identify and track users for the purposes of surveillance and call data mining if sent in the clear. Since the MEID is personally identifiable information, uses of the MEID URN with IETF protocols require a specification and IETF expert review, as described in RFC 8126, to ensure that the privacy concerns are addressed. Protocols carrying the MEID URN SHOULD, at a minimum, use strongly hop-by-hop encrypted channels, and end-to-end encryption is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The number is printed on the box and can be read off the handset, so it is not a secret and must never be used to prove that someone owns the device. It also survives a change of owner, so it must not be used to identify a person or to address messages to them.

cells: Single-mode 3GPP2 mobile equipment that supports only 3GPP2 access technology
The '3gpp2' namespace registered by this RFC

viz.caption: THE NAMESPACE SYNTAX AS DEFINED IN RFC 8464

data.title: ABNF for the 3gpp2 namespace
data.code:
pp2-urn              = "urn:" pp2-NID ":" pp2-NSS
pp2-NID              = "3gpp2"
pp2-NSS              = meid-specifier / future-pp2-specifier
meid-specifier       = "meid:" meidval
future-pp2-specifier = future-specifier *[ ":" 1*( pchar / "/" )]
future-specifier     = 1*pp2-char
pp2-char             = ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / pct-encoded

meidval           = Manufacturer-Code "-" Serial-Number
Manufacturer-Code = 8HEX
Serial-Number     = 6HEX
HEX               = DIGIT / "A" / "B" / "C" / "D" / "E" / "F"

viz.caption: THE THREE PARTS OF AN MEID

items.title: Manufacturer code
items.text: 8 hexadecimal digits. Identifies the mobile equipment manufacturer, chosen from a range allocated to it.

items.title: Serial number
items.text: 6 hexadecimal digits. Identifies the equipment within the manufacturer code.

items.title: Check digit
items.text: 1 hexadecimal digit. Catches errors when a MEID is read during inventory work. It is not transmitted and is not in the URN.
